title: wsutil: Optimize unaligned pointer access for MSVC and icc
description:
Matt Godbolt's Compiler Explorer is a useful tool for examining
what compilers actually do.

gcc and clang recognize our portable (shift-and-mask) version of
retrieving possibly unaligned values from a pointer in either
Endianness and, at -Os at higher, optimize them appropriately over
a wide variety of architectures, doing better with more recent
versions.

However, even the latest versions of MSVC and icc (both the now deprecated
Intel C++ Compiler "Classic" as well as the new LLVM based version) do not,
They do, however, optimize the memcpy based approach appropriately. The
latter, unfortunately, requires picking the right byteswap intrinsics and
avoiding treating clang-cl and icc on Windows as MSVC, since both define
_MSC_VER in the same way that they define __GNUC__ when compiling on Linux.

So for MSVC and icc and icx, use the algorithm that they manage to
optimize correctly, and use the portable version for all other
compilers, some of which (like gcc and clang) will optimize correctly.

notes.body: For what it's worth, it'll probably be a cold day in hell before Windows ever runs a processor in big-endian mode (I think Microsoft are worried about applications assuming little-endianness, although Apple managed to survive the PowerPC - x86 transition) and icc will only run on little-endian machines unless Intel either dumps x86 in favor of some big-endian ISA or decides to make a bi-endian x86 and somebody decides to run it in big-endian mode, neither of which I expect to see in my lifetime).

There is this [Intel Biendian compiler for embedded systems](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/tools/biendian-c-compiler/overview.html), which is supposed to take code written for big endian systems and produce Intel compatible binaries, but I have no idea if it would work for compiling Wireshark and if anyone would try. (I don't recall if icc, when it supported IA-64, ever could compile in Big Endian mode.)

I did consider getting rid of the checks and just assuming Little Endian for these two paths. It doesn't really hurt anything, though.

> take code written for big endian systems and produce Intel compatible binaries

Presumably by inserting `bswap` and `bswap64` instructions as needed, which I guess you could call "big-endian mode in software".

> but I have no idea if it would work for compiling Wireshark and if anyone would try

It would probably only work if you had an OS also built with that compiler, which would probably require some amount of porting to a "big-endian x86 processor".  I think that lowers the chances that anybody would try.

> I don't recall if icc, when it supported IA-64, ever could compile in Big Endian mode.

As far as I know, HP-UX ran IA-64 processors in big-endian mode, for compatibility with PA-RISC systems (PA-RISC originally was big-endian only; the 1.1 version added bi-endian support, I think for use with Windows NT).

If Intel offered the IA-64 compiler for HP-UX, that would have produced big-endian code; otherwise, I don't think any other OSes running on IA-64 were big-endian (I think Linux went little-endian, and I'd be surprised if *any* version of NT ran big-endian).

For what it's worth, MSVC also has [`__unaligned` as a pointer modifier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/cpp/unaligned?view=msvc-140) that tells the compiler that the pointer's value is not guaranteed to be naturally aligned.

However, they say "The `__unaligned` modifier isn't valid for the x86 platform.", which, if it truly means "32-bit and 64-bit x86 compilers will report an error if you use `__unaligned``", seems a bit stupid - just ignore it, so you can use it in portable-to-MSVC code!

The header at http://www.codemachine.com/downloads/win10.1607/winnt.h appears to be a Microsoft header, and defines `UNALIGNED` as `__unaligned` for a bunch of platforms (MIPS (`_M_MRX000`), Alpha, PowerPC, IA-64, x86-64, ARM, and ARM64; that includes x86-64, so maybe by "for the x86 platform" really means "for 32-bit x86"), and defines `UNALIGNED64` as `__unaligned` on 64-bit platforms (I'm not sure what happens if you have a `long long int *` and it's not guaranteed to be aligned).  I'm not sure why they do that for PPC, as I think most if not all PPC processors do unaligned accesses Just Fine by default; maybe earlier ones didn't, and the NT-on-PPC stuff may date back to that era.

I don't know whether there are any compilers for MIPS, Alpha, PA-RISC, or IA-64, other than GCC, that support enough of C11 to compile current Wireshark.  Sufficiently-recent versions of GCC seems to do unaligned-load optimization on MIPS; I don't know what they do the other platforms.  If there are, and we care enough about those platforms (none of which are currently used to build general-purpose computers, and all of which are now pretty much dead, with MIPSco deciding that RISC-V is the future), see [tcpdump's extract.h](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/tcpdump/blob/master/extract.h) (quick, before tcpdump ceases to care enough about those platforms and that stuff is flushed...).

...not that NT-on-{PPC,MIPS} matter to us, because I think the last version of NT that supported them was 4.0, for which we long ago dropped support.  All the remaining platforms that we support are 64-bit, so if we were to use `__unaligned` we wouldn't have to worry about lack of support with 64-bit data types.
